newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto offers peace to Pakistan poll victor Sharif.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto offers peace to Pakistan poll victor Sharif.

text.p: Pakistan's ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto on Tuesday refused to accept her crushing election defeat, but offered to cooperate with her victorious rival Nawaz Sharif for political stability.
She told her first news conference after Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League (PML) swept Monday's elections that the vote was a fraud engineered by a hostile caretaker government.
"I do not accept the results," she said.
Foreign election observers say they saw nothing that would have altered the outcome -- a stinging defeat for Bhutto.

In an apparent olive branch to Sharif after years of acrimony between them, Bhutto said: "Irrespective of my views concerning the legitimacy of the electoral process, I wish Mian Nawaz Sharif good luck. The country needs political stability, our people need economic relief."

She said she would propose at a meeting of her Pakistan People's Party (PPP) leaders on Wednesday that it cooperate in creating stability "which in the long run will strengthen democracy and the economic wellbeing of our people".

Bhutto spoke soon after Sharif urged her to accept defeat gracefully, as his party and its allies seemed headed for the two-thirds majority in the 217-seat National Assembly (lower house) that would enable it to change the constitution.
"I see no reason why she should not accept these results," Sharif said in Lahore, where jubilant supporters thronged his sprawling residence, dancing, beating drums and singing.

With results declared for 194 National Assembly seats, the PML had won 132 seats. With eight seats won by its ally, the Awami National Party based in North West Frontier province, it was only three seats away from a two-thirds majority of 145.

Bhutto, whose PPP had by then won only 17 seats, said Sharif could use his parliamentary clout to amend the constitution to get rid of the controversial Eighth Amendment used by presidents to dismiss four prime ministers in eight years.

"She (Bhutto) must accept the verdict of the people of Pakistan," Sharif said. "These were free and fair elections under the observation of foreign observers and the army, which deployed 250,000 men to ensure that there was no rigging.
"These elections were absolutely fair. She's a bad loser and she must accept this defeat."

The Karachi-based ethnic Mohajir National Movement (MQM), which boycotted the last National Assembly election in 1993, won 12 seats, while a breakaway PPP faction led by Bhutto's estranged sister-in-law Ghinwa Bhutto gained one seat.
Charismatic cricketer-turned-politician Imran Khan failed to win in any constituency where results had been declared.
President Farooq Leghari, once a Bhutto ally, called the polls after sacking her government on November 5, alleging corruption and misrule. Bhutto denies the charges.
Sharif, a Lahore-based industrialist who led Pakistan from 1990 to 1993, said the PML would restore stability.
"This country needs a strong and stable government and we have a very strong mandate," he said.

He said his first priority for the economy would be to deliver "clean, good, honest government" that would aim to cut spending, create an investment climate to attract foreign and domestic investors, and rationalise the tax system.

Turnout was low in Monday's elections at the end of a lacklustre campaign during the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan. No official figures were available, but commentators said it was between 30 and 40 percent of the 56.5 million eligible voters.
Polling was largely peaceful, but 10 people were killed in election day violence around the country, officials said.
The Karachi stock market welcomed the election result with a buying spree that sent the 100-share index soaring 50.74 points, or 3.18 percent, to close at 1,648 points, dealers said.
